mcqs.q: Analgesics relieve pain:
mcqs.explain: Analgesics relieve pain by acting on central or peripheral pain mechanisms without loss of consciousness.

mcqs.q: In dentistry, the FIRST-LINE analgesics for pain and inflammation are:
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs are first-line for dental pain and inflammation (caries, abscess, extraction); opioids are reserved and used minimally.

mcqs.q: Opium is extracted from:
mcqs.explain: Opium comes from the poppy (Papaver somniferum); morphine was isolated from it in the early 1800s.

mcqs.q: Most opioid analgesia (and respiratory depression and euphoria) results from action at the:
mcqs.explain: Opioids act on μ, κ and δ receptors; analgesia, respiratory depression and euphoria come mainly from μ-receptor action.

mcqs.q: The main cause of death in opioid overdose is:
mcqs.explain: Respiratory depression is the main cause of opioid-overdose death, especially dangerous when combined with alcohol.

mcqs.q: Opioid-induced nausea and vomiting are caused by stimulation of the:
opts: Chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) in the medulla
mcqs.explain: Opioids stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the medulla, producing nausea and vomiting.

mcqs.q: A classic sign of acute morphine (opioid) poisoning is:
mcqs.explain: Morphine poisoning shows respiratory depression, pinpoint miosis, cyanosis, hypotension and coma.

mcqs.q: The specific antagonist used to reverse opioid overdose is:
mcqs.explain: Naloxone is the specific opioid antagonist; management also includes airway/oxygen and blood-pressure support.

mcqs.q: Which is an opioid analgesic?
mcqs.explain: Opioid drugs include morphine, tramadol, pethidine and pentazocine; the others are NSAIDs.

mcqs.q: When opioids ARE needed for dental pain, best practice is to:
opts: Prescribe the lowest effective dose for the shortest time (~3 days)
Prescribe high doses for several weeks
mcqs.explain: Use the lowest effective dose for ≤3 days (codeine, tramadol, pentazocine), with an opioid-sparing strategy (NSAIDs + LA).

mcqs.q: Glucocorticoids (steroidal anti-inflammatories) act by inhibiting:
opts: Phospholipase A₂ (so arachidonic acid isn't formed)
mcqs.explain: Glucocorticoids inhibit phospholipase A₂, preventing arachidonic acid formation and thus all downstream prostaglandins/leukotrienes.

mcqs.q: The three major effects of NSAIDs are:
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs are anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic, all via inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX).

mcqs.q: NSAIDs produce their effects by inhibiting:
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs inhibit COX, reducing prostaglandins and thromboxanes; glucocorticoids act higher up at phospholipase A₂.

mcqs.q: Inhibition of COX-1 is responsible for which NSAID effect?
opts: Side effects — gastric ulcers, bleeding and renal failure
mcqs.explain: COX-1 is constitutive; inhibiting it causes the side effects (ulcers, bleeding, renal failure). COX-2 inhibition gives the benefits.

mcqs.q: Inhibition of COX-2 produces the BENEFICIAL effects of:
mcqs.explain: COX-2 is inducible at sites of inflammation; inhibiting it reduces inflammation, pain and fever — hence selective COX-2 inhibitors.

mcqs.q: Besides analgesia, aspirin is also used as a(n):
mcqs.explain: Aspirin (a salicylate) relieves mild-moderate pain, fever and inflammation and also acts as an antiplatelet drug; it causes no sedation/tolerance.

mcqs.q: Aspirin must be avoided in children because of the risk of:
mcqs.explain: Aspirin in children is linked to Reye's syndrome — a rare but serious swelling of the liver and brain.

mcqs.q: Salicylism (aspirin toxicity) is characterised by:
mcqs.explain: Salicylism is a syndrome of tinnitus, vertigo, decreased hearing and sometimes nausea/vomiting from aspirin overdose.

mcqs.q: Compared with aspirin and ibuprofen, paracetamol (acetaminophen):
opts: Has no significant anti-inflammatory effect and risks hepatotoxicity in overdose
mcqs.explain: Paracetamol is analgesic/antipyretic with little anti-inflammatory effect and no GI irritation, but high doses cause severe hepatotoxicity.

mcqs.q: A SELECTIVE COX-2 inhibitor is:
mcqs.explain: Celecoxib is a selective COX-2 inhibitor; aspirin, ibuprofen and diclofenac are non-selective.

mcqs.q: NSAIDs are CONTRAINDICATED in:
opts: Bleeding disorders, peptic ulcer and pregnancy
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs are contraindicated in bleeding disorders, peptic ulcers, pregnancy and asthmatics; renal and CV toxicity are concerns.

mcqs.q: Which NSAID causes FEWER GI disturbances than aspirin and is a common dental first-line drug?
mcqs.explain: Ibuprofen causes fewer GI disturbances and bleeding events than aspirin, making it a common dental first-line analgesic.

mcqs.q: For MILD post-procedural dental pain, the recommended regimen is:
mcqs.explain: Mild pain: single-agent ibuprofen 200–400 mg as needed; severe pain escalates to ibuprofen + paracetamol ± hydrocodone.

mcqs.q: For MODERATE-to-SEVERE dental pain, an effective combination is:
opts: Ibuprofen plus acetaminophen (± an opioid such as hydrocodone)
mcqs.explain: Combining ibuprofen with acetaminophen (adding hydrocodone for severe pain) gives strong multimodal analgesia with lower opioid need.

saqs.q: Classify analgesics with an example of each class.
saqs.a: Opioid/narcotic: morphine. Non-narcotic: steroidal (prednisolone) and non-steroidal NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen).

saqs.q: Name the opioid receptors and the main effects mediated by mu.
saqs.a: Receptors: μ (mu), κ (kappa), δ (delta). The μ receptor mediates analgesia, respiratory depression and euphoria.

saqs.q: Describe opioid overdose and its treatment.
saqs.a: Signs: respiratory depression, pinpoint miosis, cyanosis, hypotension, coma. Treatment: airway + oxygen, support BP, and the antagonist naloxone.

saqs.q: Differentiate the consequences of COX-1 vs COX-2 inhibition.
saqs.a: COX-1 inhibition → side effects (gastric ulcers, bleeding, renal failure). COX-2 inhibition → benefits (↓ inflammation, pain, fever).
Aspirin: analgesic/anti-inflammatory/antipyretic + antiplatelet; Reye's (children), salicylism. Paracetamol: analgesic/antipyretic, no anti-inflammatory, hepatotoxic in overdose.

saqs.q: How should opioids be used (if at all) in dentistry?
saqs.a: Minimal use; NSAIDs first-line. If needed, codeine/tramadol/pentazocine at the lowest dose for ≤3 days with an opioid-sparing approach (NSAIDs + LA).

saqs.q: Outline the dental analgesic ladder from mild to severe pain.
saqs.a: Mild: ibuprofen 200–400 mg PRN. Mild-mod: ibuprofen 400–600 mg q6h. Moderate: + paracetamol 500 mg. Severe: + hydrocodone.
